steps.caption: Before balancing, District 4 is furthest from Colorado's ideal, so its border is checked first. These 24 blocks are one stretch of that border, where it meets District 1, 154.7 km from the first move, picked because all three checks show up here.
The 11 outlined blocks are on that border: District 4 blocks touching District 1, and District 1 blocks touching District 4. Each could move to the other side.
A block may move only if it has people. 6 of them have no people.
A move must narrow the gap between the two districts, here 222 people. Here 3 moves would take people from District 1 into District 4, which already has more, so they would widen it.
District 4 must stay one connected piece. Without this block it would split, cutting off the 1 dotted block, so it stays.
That leaves 1 allowed move here, all into District 1. Along District 4's whole border, 192 of 728 moves are allowed.
Colorado's ideal is 721,714.25 people per district. Each bar is how far a district is from it before balancing: above the line is over, below is under.
Distance counts either way. District 4 is 112.75 over and District 1 is 109.25 under, so District 4 is further.
District 4 goes first. The first real move takes 70 people out of District 4 and into District 3.

If two districts are exactly as far, the one whose first block comes first in GEOID order goes first. Hawaii's two districts are each 5.50 people from its ideal of 727,635.50, one over and one under, so District 1 goes first.
Colorado has 5,773,714 people and 8 seats.
5,773,714 / 8 = 721,714.25 people per district, which no district can hit exactly.
So the target is the two neighboring whole numbers: 721,714 and 721,715. Each bar is a district's final distance from the ideal, and 7 of 8 are within one person of it.
Each bar is a district's distance from Colorado's ideal of 721,714.25, before move 16 (left) and before move 17 (right). Before move 16, District 2 is furthest, 2.25 under, so it is tried first.
None of the 762 moves on its border is allowed: 188 are blocks with no people and 574 would widen a gap.

Districts 1, 3, 5 and 8 border it, larger by 3, 3, 2 and 0 people. A move narrows a gap only if it carries fewer people than the gap, but the smallest blocks with people that could cross into it hold 11, 8, 10 and 26.
So the pass tries the next furthest district. That is District 8, 2.25 under.
District 8 has 10 allowed moves. The best moves 2 people into District 8 from District 7: that is move 16.
After every move the pass starts again from the furthest district. Before move 17, that is District 2 again, 2.25 under, still with no allowed move, so District 4, the next furthest, makes move 17.
In Colorado, District 4 is 112.75 over the ideal of 721,714.25 and District 3 is 29.25 under. These are the 24 blocks nearest the block that moves first.
The 4 outlined blocks may move from District 4 into District 3. Each move is scored by how much it lowers the sum of the squared differences from the ideal.
The best is this block of 70 people: 2 × 70 × (112.75 − -29.25 − 70) = 10,080. The next best allowed move anywhere on District 4's border scores 10,074.
So it moves into District 3. District 4 now has 721,757 people and District 3 has 721,755, and the sum falls by exactly 10,080.
Before balancing, Colorado's districts run from 721,605 to 721,827 people, a range of 222. Squaring each district's distance from the ideal 721,714.25 and adding up gives 33,609.50.
Each of the 17 moves lowers that sum, the first by 10,080 and the last by 2. Each dot is the sum after a move.
After 17 moves the sum is 7.50 and the range is 3.
No move lowers the sum any further, so the pass stops. It always does: every move lowers the sum by at least 2, and a sum of squares never goes below zero.
Alabama has 7 seats, so its first cut splits them 3 and 4. Take the direction cut 1 is drawn at, 84.6° from north-south.
First with the 3 seats north of the line and 4 south: the line falls here, and its border is 474,793 m long.
Then the same direction with the 3 seats south of the line and 4 north: the line moves, and its border is 659,208 m long.
The shorter way is kept, with the 3 seats north of the line: 474,793 m against 659,208 m.
Colorado, small in the middle, on a plain grid of longitude and latitude, with the parallel at 39° north and the meridian at 106° west running through it.
This is cut 3's guide line, continued past the state along its great circle for 2,500 km each way. On this grid it bows: its middle sits 451 km off the straight path between its ends.
The generator measures directions in a flat projection centered on the state. In it every great circle, the path a plane through the Earth's center traces on the surface, is a straight line.
Here the guide line is exactly straight, and so is the meridian, which is also a great circle. The parallel is not a great circle, so it curves.
Cut 3 in Colorado, near the middle of its line. Every block is now on the first side or the second, shaded by side.
The border is every block edge with a first-side block on one hand and a second-side block on the other. These 19 edges measure 726 m.
Adding the next 19 edges brings it to 1,041 m.
All 55 border edges in view add up to 1,349 m, each measured along the surface of the Earth.
Along the whole line, 1,494 such edges add up to 55,455 m. That is the length of cut 3's border. Water inside the state counts as part of the state, so a bay or lake would not shorten this border.
Cut 3 in Colorado splits a piece of 29,914 blocks. These are the 20 blocks nearest the middle of its line.
Each block has an internal point, a spot inside it that the Census Bureau publishes.
What orders the blocks is how far each point sits across the line, measured at right angles to it.
Sorted by that distance, these 20 line up like this. In the full walk they fall between places 20,601 and 21,451.
The walk adds up people in this order. 9 of these blocks come before it stops and join the first side; the other 11 start the second side.
No two of the 29,914 blocks sit at exactly the same distance. If two did, the one with the smaller GEOID would come first.

Florida's first cut tries every straight line. Turning the line, the directions fall into stretches: every direction inside one stretch splits the people the same way. Cut 1 has 437,327 such stretches. Each tick is one of the 200 leading stretches (the best few from every part of the half turn), in order of direction, at the length of its border.
Each stretch is checked once, however wide it is. Its line is first settled for stray pieces, and only then is its real border measured. Each tick is that measured length.
Now the stretches are sorted by border length, shortest first.
Not every stretch can be used. 17 shorter border lengths belong to stretches that are shorter still but whose two sides are not each one connected piece. They are skipped, and are not drawn here.

The shortest stretch left, 80.3357° to 80.3367° from north-south at 402.3 km, has two connected sides, so it is the cut. The guide line is drawn through its middle, 80.3362°. It is the 80.3362° and 402,273 m of cut 1 on the real map.
Alabama has 5,024,279 people and 7 seats, so the first cut works on all 7.
The 7 seats split into 3 and 4. The 3-seat side should hold 3 of every 7 people.
5,024,279 x 3 / 7 = 2,153,262.43, the number of people the 3-seat side should hold.
Searching every cut in all 50 states: in 10 of 385 cuts the two best borders are exactly equal, to the micrometer. The one on the fewest blocks is Massachusetts's cut 6.
Massachusetts's cut 6 splits 4 seats. Its two best borders belong to the stretches of directions 178.4769° to 178.4812° and 178.4769° to 178.4808° from north-south.
Both stretches give exactly the same border length, so they are tied.

The rule is shortest border, then the sides nearer their fair shares of people, then GEOID. Both stretches give the same two sides, so they are one cut and nothing needs deciding. The guide line is drawn in the first stretch clockwise from north, 178.4769° to 178.4812°.
So the cut is the stretch 178.4769° to 178.4812°. Its guide line is drawn through the middle, 178.479°. On the real map, Massachusetts cut 6 is 178.479° and 111,756 m.
Cut 3 in Colorado: the first side's share is 721,626 people. Walking in order, the first 20,971 blocks add up to 721,528, still short.
Next in the walk is this block, with 619 people.
With it the total is 722,147, past the share, so the walk stops at this block.
Before it the total is 98 short of the share; after it, 521 over. After is not strictly closer, so the block starts the second side.
The guide line on the map sits between the last free block of the first side and the first free block of the second, measured across the line.
Run the generator on Colorado and fingerprint the plan with SHA-256.
Run it again from scratch and fingerprint that plan too.
The two fingerprints are identical, so the two plans are identical.
Two blocks in Colorado, the first pair in GEOID order that touch only at a corner: 080010078011000 and 080010078011012.
They meet at this single point and share no edge. Touching at a corner does not count, so these two are not connected.
This block, 080010078011001, shares an edge with the first one, marked along its length, so those two are connected.
The line chosen for cut 2 in Colorado, 90.3° from north-south. Its strays take 3 passes to settle; each dot is a block that moves in one of them.
Pass 1. After the walk, 9 blocks are cut off from their side and move, each fixed at once. 3 of them are highlighted here, close up.
Pass 2. The re-count walks the free blocks again, and 2 more blocks are cut off. They are highlighted here, close up. Dots mark blocks fixed earlier.
Pass 3 moves no free block, so it ends: 3 walks, 11 fixed blocks, and the line slid 1 meter in all. A piece of 66,825 blocks could need at most 66,825 walks.
Cut 1 in Colorado, just after its first walk. These 2 blocks are on the first side, cut off from the rest of it.
They join the second side, the side around them, and are fixed to it at once. A dot marks each fixed block.
The re-count walks the free blocks again. By position these 2 would fall on the first side, but fixed blocks are left out of the walk, so they stay on the second side.
No later pass can move them either. They end cut 1 on the second side, where they were fixed.

Fixed blocks count toward their side's groups like any other block. On a line tried for cut 11 in Georgia at 37.2°, this group on the first side holds 1 block fixed there (dotted) and 2 blocks still free, and it is cut off from the side's main body.
Its free blocks join the second side. Its fixed block stays on the first side, where it was fixed.
Alaska has 49 pieces of land that share no edge with the rest: islands and other detached land. This island is 2 blocks.
The nearest block of the main body is 12.1 km away, measured between internal points.
The two blocks are joined as if they shared an edge, so the island counts as connected to the rest of Alaska.
Detached land is connected one shortest link at a time, measured between internal points and often to another island, so Alaska can be cut like any other state.
A line tried for cut 5 in Virginia, 13.2° from north-south. After walk 2, these 1 blocks are on the first side, cut off from it.
They join the second side, the side around them, and are fixed there. A dot marks each fixed block.
After the re-count, these 1 are cut off from the second side again.
Pass 12 moves no free block, and these 1 cannot move back: they are fixed. The second side is left in more than one piece.
So this line's second side is not one connected piece. It fails that check, and the next shortest line is considered.
Cut 3 in Colorado splits this piece, with 2 seats, into 1 and 1. The outline is the edge of the piece's blocks.
Its line runs here, 135.4° from north-south.
The line crosses the piece's outline 4 times, marked: it leaves the piece and comes back in. At this scale some of the marks sit almost on top of each other.
Up close: the line leaves the piece, runs 0.7 km outside it (dashed), and comes back in.
That is allowed. A line may cross the piece's outline any number of times.
Cut 2 in Colorado, just after its first walk. These 2 blocks are on the second side, cut off from the rest of it.
They join the first side and are fixed there with their 128 people. With 4 more blocks fixed elsewhere, 261 people are fixed on the first side.
The first side's share is 1,443,382 people. The 261 fixed people already count on it.
So the re-count walks the free blocks only, in the same order, toward 1,443,382 minus 261: a target of 1,443,121.
The walk stops by the same rule, and the guide line moves to between the last free block of the first side and the first free block of the second: here by 1 meter.
Cut 1 in Colorado, just after its first walk, shaded by side. These 2 blocks are on the first side, but no edge links them to the rest of it.
After the walk the first side is in 6 connected groups. Its main body is the group with the most people: 2,886,602 in 73,519 blocks.
This group has 324 people in 2 blocks, so it is not the main body. The lower GEOID would only decide a tie in people.
Every group other than the main body joins the second side, the side around it: here 5 groups with 6 blocks, this one included.
Then the second side is settled the same way, and 2 groups with 4 blocks cut off from it join the first side. This repeats until nothing moves.
